Something about the library as a whole.

docs.title: LibraryVersionError
docs.text:
Bases: LibraryError, LibraryVersionError

The library on disk was written by a different build (see db.SCHEMA_VERSION). Refused rather than opened, because a library this build cannot read must be left exactly as it was found.

docs.title: MediaCompostError
docs.text:
Bases: Exception

Base class for everything this API raises.

docs.title: MediaUnreadable
docs.text:
Bases: MediaCompostError, OSError

ffmpeg could not read these bytes.

Its own class because a caller walking a whole library has to be able to skip one broken film without catching everything: one unreadable file is a line in a log, not the end of a run. Item.frames() translates the core media error into this, so nothing outside the package has to know that error exists.

docs.title: NotFound
docs.text:
Bases: MediaCompostError, KeyError

No such row.

Subclasses KeyError so a Mapping behaves as one — but with a readable str(), because KeyError's repr-of-the-argument turns a sentence into a quoted mess.

docs.title: ObjectDeleted
docs.text:
Bases: NotFound

The row behind this handle is gone.

Raised on the next read AND on any write, never silently tolerated: an exporter that keeps writing files for an item somebody deleted mid-run is a bug you find in the output rather than the traceback.

docs.title: ReadOnlyError
docs.text:
Bases: LibraryError

A write on a library opened with mode="r".

docs.title: UnsupportedOperation
docs.text:
Bases: MediaCompostError, ValueError

The object does not do that — frames() on a still, say.

docs.title: ValidationError
docs.text:
Bases: MediaCompostError, ValueError

The input is malformed.

docs.title: Appearance
docs.text:
Appearance(lib, row_id: int, row: Optional[T] = None)

Bases: Handle

One "this person is in this picture", optionally at one face.

Several per item is the point: the same character twice on a page, at two ages. The AGE is a fact about the picture, not about the name on it.

docs.title: rect property writable
docs.text:
rect: Optional[Rect]

The appearance's SUBJECT BOX — the whole figure, where the face is only the head. None until somebody draws one.

docs.title: points property writable
docs.text:
points: Optional[list]

The subject box's optional polygon (Box.points' rule: while one is set, rect is its bounding box).

docs.title: guessed property
docs.text:
guessed: bool

A machine said this and nobody has agreed yet.

docs.title: confirm
docs.text:
confirm() -> None

Agree with a guess. Its pending tag stops being pending, which is what lets search, training and export see it at last.

docs.title: Artifact
docs.text:
Artifact(lib, row_id: int, row: Optional[T] = None)

Bases: Handle

Something generated from a file and stored beside it — a depth map, a pose overlay, a cached training latent.

docs.title: stale property
docs.text:
stale: bool

True when the source file was edited after this was generated.

docs.title: rel_path property
docs.text:
rel_path: str

Where this sits inside the item's folder — the name File.artifact_name produces.

docs.title: parent property
docs.text:
parent: Optional['Artifact']

The artifact this one was made FROM, when it was not made from the file itself — a latent cached off a degraded copy points at that copy, so deleting the copy takes its latents with it.

docs.title: Box
docs.text:
Box(lib, row_id: int, row: Optional[T] = None)

Bases: Handle

A rectangle, a time range, or both, hanging off a tag on an item.

docs.title: points property writable
docs.text:
points: Optional[list]

The box's optional POLYGON — [[x, y], ...] vertices in the item's reference frame. While one is set, rect is its bounding box (the server keeps the two in step). None for a plain rectangle.

docs.title: negative property
docs.text:
negative: bool

A TIME RANGE carries its own sign: over a film a tag is present in some stretches and pointedly absent in others.

docs.title: Caption
docs.text:
Caption(lib, row_id: int, row: Optional[T] = None)

Bases: Handle

One caption on an item.

docs.title: tags property
docs.text:
tags: NameSet

The caption's META tags — the app's own namespace, which never reaches a picture's tags, search or training.

docs.title: kind property
docs.text:
kind: str

"caption" (what the picture is) or "instruction" (how it was made from the items in refs). Fixed when the row is created.

docs.title: refs property writable
docs.text:
refs: list

An instruction's source images, IN ORDER. Empty for a caption.

docs.title: pending property
docs.text:
pending: bool

True for a machine-written caption nobody has agreed to yet.

docs.title: approve
docs.text:
approve() -> None

Agree with a machine's caption as it stands. Editing one approves it too; this is the button for when it needed no changing.

docs.title: Event
docs.text:
Event(lib, row_id: int, row: Optional[T] = None)

Bases: Handle

What was happening — a span of days on a tag.

The MODEL is called Occasion, because Event is the modification log's row. The UI, the routes and this API all say "event"; only the ORM diverges, and this is where that stops mattering.

docs.title: comment property writable
docs.text:
comment: str

The identity TAG's, like a subject's and a place's.

docs.title: span
docs.text:
span(start=None, end=None) -> None

Set when it was. Either side may be None to leave it alone.

docs.title: places property
docs.text:
places: HandleSet

Where it was. Every one must be NAMED — a venue is a tag on no item at all more often than not, and an unnamed place has no name for anything to refer to it by.

docs.title: Face
docs.text:
Face(lib, row_id: int, row: Optional[T] = None)

Bases: Handle

A crop a detector found, or a hand drew.

Evidence, not an edit: it keeps its box, its score and its descriptor forever, named or not, and a re-run never loses work.

docs.title: outline property
docs.text:
outline: Optional[Rect]

The face's optional OUTLINE — the whole figure, drawn by hand, where the face box is only the head. A subject attached to the face uses it wherever it has no subject box of its own.

docs.title: outline_points property
docs.text:
outline_points: Optional[list]

The outline's polygon (Box.points' rule: outline is then its bounding box).

docs.title: det_score property
docs.text:
det_score: Optional[float]

How sure the detector was. None for a face somebody drew.

docs.title: models property
docs.text:
models: tuple[str, ...]

Every detector that found this face — one head, one rectangle, so several models may agree on it.

docs.title: appearances property
docs.text:
appearances: tuple[Appearance, ...]

Every claim on this face — who, how sure, and how old they are in it. A face may be several people at once, so this is a tuple.

docs.title: subjects property
docs.text:
subjects: tuple[Subject, ...]

Just the people, which is what the name promises.

This used to return the Appearance rows, so face.subjects[0] .display_name — the obvious line — raised. Item already had the pair, and Face disagreeing with it was one word doing two jobs.

docs.title: name
docs.text:
name(who, *, comment: str = '') -> 'Face'

Say who this is — ADDING a claim, not replacing one.

A face may be several people at once (a drawn character and the actor who plays them), so this appends. unname takes one off, and is remembered differently: taking off a machine's GUESS records a refusal so the next run does not offer it again.

docs.title: crop
docs.text:
crop(*, margin: float = 0.25)

The face as a PIL image, cut out of its item's picture.

docs.title: File
docs.text:
File(lib, row_id: int, row: Optional[T] = None)

Bases: Handle

One version of an item's bytes.

docs.title: number property
docs.text:
number: Optional[int]

The stable per-item source number (#1, #2, …) — what names the file on disk.

docs.title: phash property
docs.text:
phash: Optional[str]

The perceptual hash dedup compares. None for a video.

docs.title: rotation property
docs.text:
rotation: int

Which way these bytes sit relative to the item's FIRST source file.

Provenance, not a transform to apply: the pixels are already turned. width/height are likewise already in this orientation.

docs.title: crop property
docs.text:
crop: Rect

This file's region of the item's reference frame.

docs.title: source_kind property
docs.text:
source_kind: str

stored | video_frame | video_clip.

docs.title: frame_rate property
docs.text:
frame_rate: Optional[float]

Frames per second, for a video. None when nothing probed it — which is a real state, not a zero: no ffprobe on the machine means a film imports with no duration and no rate at all.

docs.title: path property
docs.text:
path: Optional[Path]

Where the bytes are on disk. None when the row has no stored file.

This is the answer to "there is no export, but let me at the files".

docs.title: image
docs.text:
image()

The pixels as a PIL image.

The stored bytes are ALREADY in their final orientation — rotating an item writes a new file with the turned pixels — so rotation is provenance (which way these bytes sit relative to the item's first source file), not something to apply. Opening the path and rotating by it would turn every rotated picture twice.

docs.title: sources property
docs.text:
sources: HandleList

Every recorded source of these bytes.

docs.title: add_source
docs.text:
add_source(name: str) -> FileSource

Record a filename this file was seen under.

docs.title: add_url
docs.text:
add_url(url: str, *, accessed_at=None) -> FileSource

Record a web address these bytes came from, and when.

THE PROVENANCE CALL for an import: ImportResult.file names the stored file a source landed on — the EXISTING one for a duplicate, which is the case worth recording (one picture at a second address) — so got.file.add_url(url, accessed_at=fetched) is the line after every imported download. Idempotent per (url, access time): re-recording the same fetch answers the existing row, so a re-crawl needs no try/except; the same URL at a DIFFERENT time is a second, genuinely different record. An offset-aware time is stored as the UTC moment it names.

docs.title: artifact_name
docs.text:
artifact_name(kind: str, key: str = '', ext: str = 'bin') -> str

The item-folder-relative name an artifact of this file WOULD have.

Creates nothing and touches no disk. key is whatever makes one rendering different from another — a model, a size, a set of drawn parameters — and may be composed out of pieces; it is slugged, so which characters survive is not the caller's problem.

docs.title: artifact_path
docs.text:
artifact_path(kind: str, key: str = '', ext: str = 'bin') -> Path

artifact_name as an absolute path — what you hand to a process that will write the bytes itself. The folder is created.

docs.title: find_artifact
docs.text:
find_artifact(kind: str, *, model: str = '', name: str = '') -> Optional['Artifact']

The recorded artifact of this kind (and model, and stored name), or None. This is the cache lookup.

Note it answers about the ROW. A row whose bytes have since been pruned still answers, which is why a cache that cares checks artifact.path too — the two can disagree, and re-encoding is cheaper than reading a file that is not there.

docs.title: add_artifact
docs.text:
add_artifact(kind: str, data: bytes, *, key: str = '', ext: str = '', model: str = '', width: int = 0, height: int = 0, parent: Optional['Artifact'] = None) -> 'Artifact'

Store data at artifact_name(kind, key, ext) and record it.

docs.title: record_artifact
docs.text:
record_artifact(kind: str, *, key: str = '', ext: str = '', model: str = '', width: int = 0, height: int = 0, parent: Optional['Artifact'] = None) -> Optional['Artifact']

Record bytes ALREADY on disk at artifact_path(kind, key, ext).

For a file another process wrote — a trainer caching a tensor the library could not have produced. Returns None when nothing is there, and the existing handle when the row already exists, so running it again over a folder adds nothing.

docs.title: split_out
docs.text:
split_out() -> 'Item'

Move this file into an item of its own, linked back to this one.

For when the deduper grouped genuinely different pictures as versions of each other.

docs.title: delete
docs.text:
delete() -> None

Remove this version, its bytes, its artifacts and its thumbnail.

docs.title: FileSource
docs.text:
FileSource(lib, row_id: int, row: Optional[T] = None)

Bases: Handle

Where a stored file's bytes came from: a filename with its import path, or a web URL with the time it was fetched.

docs.title: Group
docs.text:
Group(lib, row_id: int, row: Optional[T] = None)

Bases: Handle

A library group. Groups form a TREE — one parent at most.

docs.title: smart_query property writable
docs.text:
smart_query: str

The SMART group's membership rule (the saved-search tag set); "" for an ordinary group too, since it has none. Smart is an IDENTITY fixed at creation (groups.create(smart_query=…)): assigning here edits a smart group's rule — refused on an ordinary group, and a smart group stays smart whatever the rule says (an empty rule holds nothing).

docs.title: path property
docs.text:
path: str

Trips/2019/Japan — the names from the root down.

docs.title: items property
docs.text:
items

Items directly in this group.

docs.title: tags property
docs.text:
tags: NameSet

Tags this group GRANTS its items — inherited by the whole subtree.

The highest-leverage write in the API: one assignment tags everything under it, and it is where most of a library's inherited tags come from.

docs.title: add
docs.text:
add(items) -> int

Put items in this group (bulk — one call, one event each).

docs.title: duplicate
docs.text:
duplicate(parent=None) -> 'Group'

A deep copy of this group and its subtree, sharing the items.

docs.title: delete
docs.text:
delete(*, assign_tags: bool = False) -> None

Delete the group. assign_tags bakes what it granted onto its items first, so they keep the tags they were inheriting.

docs.title: Item
docs.text:
Item(lib, row_id: int, row: Optional[T] = None)

Bases: Handle

One picture, video or sequence container — everything else hangs off it.

docs.title: uid property
docs.text:
uid: str

The stable identity that names the item's folder on disk and every cross-item reference in an export or a merge. Survives export and re-import.

docs.title: kind property
docs.text:
kind: str

image | video | sequence.

docs.title: created_at property
docs.text:
created_at

First time it was seen in the library.

docs.title: taken property writable
docs.text:
taken

When the picture was taken, as SOMEBODY SAID it — the override.

Three states, which is why NEVER exists: None means nobody has said (read the file, then the events it carries), a date means somebody typed one, and NEVER means somebody looked and there is none. Without the third a wrong EXIF date could be replaced but never removed.

docs.title: taken_effective property
docs.text:
taken_effective: Optional[PartialDate]

What the library concludes, walking the three answers in order: what somebody typed, the indexed EXIF date, then the span of the events this picture carries.

docs.title: taken_source property
docs.text:
taken_source: str

set | exif | event | never | "" — which of the three answered.

docs.title: active_file property writable
docs.text:
active_file: Optional[File]

The version everything reads — thumbnail, preview, metadata, export.

docs.title: path property
docs.text:
path: Optional[Path]

The active file's bytes on disk.

docs.title: image
docs.text:
image()

The active file as a PIL image, in its final orientation.

docs.title: frames
docs.text:
frames(fps: Optional[float] = None, *, max_dim: Optional[int] = None) -> Iterator

(index, timestamp, PIL.Image) decoded straight from a video.

Nothing is written to the library, which is what makes this the way to turn a film into training images inside an exporter.

max_dim caps the long side — ffmpeg downscales, never upscales, and the aspect is kept. A consumer that only needs a bucket-sized picture pays neither the decode nor the scratch space of a 4K frame, and a perceptual hash is unaffected by the reduction.

docs.title: tags property writable
docs.text:
tags: TagSet

What the ITEM says — direct, positive. .negative is the sibling.

docs.title: effective_tags property
docs.text:
effective_tags: frozenset

What the LIBRARY concludes: direct + group-inherited + implied.

Read-only, and a plain frozenset so .add() fails with the stdlib's own message. Assigning goes through tags, a group's grants, or an implication — three different things in three different places.

docs.title: tag_groups property
docs.text:
tag_groups

This item's tag groupings. [...] takes a NAME and gets-or-creates (exact spelling first, else a unique case-insensitive match, else a new group — minting "hers" beside "Hers" over a shift key is the silent duplicate this avoids), so the doc's item.tag_groups["Hers"].tags.add("blue_eyes") is one line. A name two groups share raises AmbiguousName; an int is still an id, and .get(name) is the read that never creates.

docs.title: captions property
docs.text:
captions: HandleList

What the picture IS. Instructions are a separate list — mixing them is how a description ends up training an edit model.

docs.title: instructions property
docs.text:
instructions: HandleList

How the picture was MADE from others: text plus the ordered source items. Same row type as a caption, deliberately kept apart.

docs.title: add_instruction
docs.text:
add_instruction(text: str, refs: Iterable = ()) -> Caption

An instruction on this item, with the items it was made FROM.

refs is an ordered sequence of Item handles or ids; the order is the order the model is shown them.

docs.title: subjects property
docs.text:
subjects: HandleSet

Who is in this picture. Adding one assigns their identity tag — that connection is the point, since the tag is what search reads.

docs.title: add_face
docs.text:
add_face(x: float, y: float, w: float, h: float, *, subject=None) -> Face

Draw a face by hand — no detector, so no score and no descriptor, and no later run can take it away.

docs.title: face_models property
docs.text:
face_models: tuple[str, ...]

Detectors that have LOOKED at this item, whatever they found.

Not derivable from the faces: an item a model found nothing in has no face to carry the fact, and that is exactly the item a "skip what is done" sweep must not run again.

docs.title: text_blocks property
docs.text:
text_blocks: HandleList

The ACTIVE file's TOP-LEVEL text regions, in reading order; each carries its finer levels as children. Per file, the artifact rule: a reading is a fact about pixels, so an edited file made active answers with nothing until an engine reads it. Deliberately no item.text shortcut — a page's text is a rendering decision (separator, dismissed regions in or out, children flattened or not), so the one-liner is yours: "\n".join(b.text for b in item.text_blocks).

docs.title: add_text
docs.text:
add_text(x: float, y: float, w: float, h: float, *, text: str = '', level: str = 'block', parent=None) -> TextRegion

Draw a text box by hand — no engine, so no score and no model credit, and no later run can rewrite what is typed into it.

docs.title: text_models property
docs.text:
text_models: tuple[str, ...]

Text engines that have READ this item's ACTIVE file, whatever they found — face_models' twin (ItemTextRun), per file so an edited file reads as never-read.

docs.title: places property
docs.text:
places: tuple[Place, ...]

Where this was taken — derived from the tags it carries.

docs.title: links property
docs.text:
links: HandleSet

Items derived FROM this one.

docs.title: linked_by property
docs.text:
linked_by: HandleSet

Items this one derives from.

docs.title: metadata property
docs.text:
metadata: dict

Everything known about the picture: the intrinsic values computed from the active file, plus what the item answers with — its active file's own metadata and anything pinned to the item. Read-only.

ONE value per name here, the PIN winning, because this is a plain dict and a script asking item.metadata["iso"] wants an answer rather than a set. Search is the place that matches ANY of an item's values; files is where each file's own answers can be read one by one.

docs.title: rotate
docs.text:
rotate(direction='right') -> None

Turn the active image a quarter. Lossless, so repeated rotations never degrade it.

docs.title: delete
docs.text:
delete() -> None

Permanently — the files, the folder, the thumbnails. trash() is the reversible one.

docs.title: merge_from
docs.text:
merge_from(other) -> 'Item'

Fold another item into this one: its files, groups, tags and captions come across and it disappears.

docs.title: ItemTagGroup
docs.text:
ItemTagGroup(lib, row_id: int, row: Optional[T] = None)

Bases: Handle

A per-item grouping of tags — "hers", "his", or the auto-managed Pending group a generation run files its guesses into.

docs.title: system property
docs.text:
system: bool

True for the auto-managed Pending group. It takes no drops.

docs.title: meta_tags property
docs.text:
meta_tags: NameSet

Labels on the GROUPING itself. They never become tags of the item — that separation is the whole point of them.

docs.title: subjects property
docs.text:
subjects: HandleSet

Who this grouping is ABOUT — purely organizational, like the meta tags: search never learns "her hair is blonde".

docs.title: delete
docs.text:
delete() -> None

Delete the grouping; its tags fall back to Ungrouped.

docs.title: Link
docs.text:
Link(lib, row_id: int, row=None, *, outgoing: bool = True)

Bases: Handle

A directed edge between two items — an edit to what it came from, a panel to its page, a still to its film.

docs.title: flip
docs.text:
flip() -> 'Link'

Reverse which end is the original. For an edit link this re-roots the whole cluster, so "one original per item" stays true.

docs.title: MetaTag
docs.text:
MetaTag(lib, row_id: int, row: Optional[T] = None)

Bases: Handle

A name in the meta-tag namespace — the labels on links, captions and per-item tag groups. A separate namespace from item tags on purpose: these describe the annotation, not the picture, and never reach search.

docs.title: description property writable
docs.text:
description: str

The long form, with line breaks — what a ? beside the name opens. comment is the one-liner that rides beside the name.

docs.title: delete
docs.text:
delete() -> None

Remove it from every link, caption and tag group carrying it.

docs.title: Place
docs.text:
Place(lib, row_id: int, row: Optional[T] = None)

Bases: Handle

Where a picture was taken — location data on a tag.

docs.title: name property writable
docs.text:
name: str

What the place is called, as ONE line — an address, "the corner of the old market", "Bob's house". It was eight typed components with a per-country form; a place is a line somebody reads.

docs.title: parent property writable
docs.text:
parent: Optional['Place']

The place this one is IN. Assigning it implies the parents — the containment is an ordinary tag implication under the hood.

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
Sequence(lib, row_id: int, row: Optional[T] = None)

Bases: Handle

An ordered run of items — a chapter, a film's frames, a set.

docs.title: kind property
docs.text:
kind: str

How it came to be: archive | pdf | gif | manual (an older library may hold video, from a removed import option). Provenance only — all sequences behave alike, but a re-import recognises its own by it.

docs.title: item property
docs.text:
item: Optional['Item']

The CONTAINER item, so a sequence can be selected and tagged like anything else in the grid.

docs.title: members property
docs.text:
members: HandleList

The items, one entry per POSITION — a book's repeated blank page is one item listed at each of its positions. This list speaks in ITEMS: deleting one removes every occurrence, and reorder refuses a sequence that repeats an item (a list of items cannot say which copy goes where — the app's own reorder addresses membership rows).

docs.title: remove
docs.text:
remove(items) -> int

Take items out — EVERY occurrence of each; that is what "remove this picture from the chapter" means.

docs.title: delete
docs.text:
delete() -> None

Remove the sequence and its container, keeping the members.

docs.title: Subject
docs.text:
Subject(lib, row_id: int, row: Optional[T] = None)

Bases: Handle

Who or what a picture is OF — extra data on a tag.

docs.title: comment property writable
docs.text:
comment: str

What tells two people of one name apart — the identity TAG's.

docs.title: since property writable
docs.text:
since: Optional[PartialDate]

When they came into being — a birth date, a release date.

docs.title: tag property writable
docs.text:
tag: Optional[Tag]

The tag this subject IS. None for a face cluster nobody has named.

docs.title: merge_into
docs.text:
merge_into(other, *, keep_alias: bool = True) -> 'Subject'

Fold this identity into another: the faces move and the tags merge.

docs.title: delete
docs.text:
delete(*, with_tag: bool = False) -> None

Delete the identity, keeping its tag — the pictures are still of something. with_tag deletes that too.

docs.title: Tag
docs.text:
Tag(lib, row_id: int, row: Optional[T] = None)

Bases: Handle

A row in the tag catalog.

docs.title: meta_tag_counts property
docs.text:
meta_tag_counts: dict[str, int]

Pictures this tag has WHERE EACH META TAG SAYS — {"tumblr": 50, "twitter": 100}, nonzero entries only. The per-site successor of the old tag-level count_offset (one number could not say where it came from).

Never added to a count the app displays — a total that silently included it would be the app making a claim about somewhere else. What it is FOR is ordering: the autocomplete's equal-count ties sort by the highest of these. (A training run could once balance against it, under the name the tag-level offset left behind; that freq_base value is gone.)

docs.title: set_meta_tag_count
docs.text:
set_meta_tag_count(name: str, count: int) -> None

Set the count on one meta-tag assignment — assigning the meta tag first when the tag does not carry it yet. Logged and revertible like every other Tags-tab edit.

docs.title: alias_of property writable
docs.text:
alias_of: Optional['Tag']

The tag this one is a second name FOR, if any.

Assigning an alias redirects to its target, which is why an alias implies nothing of its own.

docs.title: namespace property
docs.text:
namespace: str

The text before the first colon — costume in costume:tiger.

docs.title: implies property
docs.text:
implies: NameSet

What assigning this tag also assigns, transitively.

docs.title: meta_tags property
docs.text:
meta_tags: NameSet

What the TAG SET says about this tag — "noflip", "character" — in the same namespace links, captions and tag groups use.

It never reaches a picture, so search, counts and training see no new tag; what reads it is what asks about the tag itself (TAG:noflip, and a training run refusing to mirror what carries it).

docs.title: items property
docs.text:
items

Every item this tag is effectively on.

docs.title: item_count property
docs.text:
item_count: int

How many items carry it, folded exactly as a search folds it.

len(tag.items) is the same number for a tag whose name a search can be typed for, and this is the one to reach for when it may not be: items goes through the query grammar, which LOWERCASES what it is given, so a tag whose stored name carries a capital is not found by it at all — it answers 0 for a tag on a thousand pictures. The catalog's own names are case-preserving (an import can carry one), so this matches the name as stored.

docs.title: merge_into

merge_into(other, *, keep_alias: bool = True) -> 'Tag'

ImportEntry(status: ImportStatus = SKIPPED, item: Any = None, file: Any = None, name: str = '', error: str = '', derived: bool = False, children: tuple = ())

A source yields a FLAT list of these, however deeply nested it physically was — a zip of PDFs is one entry per PDF, a zip inside a zip flattens, and a book found inside a book is a flat sibling entry rather than a member of the outer sequence (the rule that keeps the depth fixed). children go exactly one level further: the pages of a book, the frames a video matched — children of children do not exist.

docs.title: add
docs.text:
add(source: ImportSource, *, move: Optional[bool] = None) -> ImportResult

Import one ImportSource: a path (a file, a folder, an archive, a video) or an ImportBytes for in-memory data — run.add(ImportBytes(data=body, name="cat.png")). Bytes get the identical pipeline a file on disk gets; the name's extension decides how they are read, and a usable one is sniffed from the content when it is missing.

Where in-memory bytes CAME FROM is recorded afterwards, on the result: got.file is the stored file they landed on — the EXISTING one for a duplicate, which is the case worth recording — and got.file.add_url(url, accessed_at=fetched) is the same web-URL source the Source list adds by hand, idempotent per (url, time) so a re-crawl needs no bookkeeping.

move — for path sources — removes the source once it is safely ingested. It defaults to the RUN's setting: None, not False, because False here would silently override a run opened with move=True.

docs.title: add_many
docs.text:
add_many(sources: Iterable[ImportSource], *, prefetch: Optional[int] = None, processes: Optional[bool] = None) -> Iterator[ImportResult]

Import an iterable of sources, hashing ahead on workers.

Yields one ImportResult per source, in order — the same results the same sources would get from a loop of add, and the same single-writer import underneath. What is parallel is only the per-source arithmetic that reads no library state: the sha256, the decode, the perceptual hash, the colour signature, the eight orientation hashes and the metadata read of upcoming STILL IMAGES are computed on workers while the serial half stores the current one. Folders, archives, PDFs and videos take the serial path unchanged.

prefetch is how many sources may be in flight at once (default: the worker count for threads; 4x it for processes, whose queued bundles are kilobytes). A thread bundle holds its decoded pixels in memory until its turn, so a run of very large images may want it small; the worker count follows it downward, capped at min(8, CPUs) — see _pool_shape.

processes runs that half in worker PROCESSES instead of threads, so the prefetch stops competing with the importing thread for the GIL — measured over four crawl archives, the serial half alone runs 0.92 s where the same loop under 8 prefetch THREADS takes 1.66 s: the workers' GIL slices come straight out of the importing thread. It is off unless asked, and the caller must have an if __name__ == "__main__": guard — the pool has to be spawn (forking this process would fork a live SQLite connection and the library's own daemon threads into a child that never runs them), and a spawned worker re-imports its parent's __main__. Without the guard a script re-runs its own import in every worker, which starts more workers: a fork bomb, instantly. Nothing here can detect that, which is why this cannot default to True.

What it costs is a one-time ~0.4 s pool start (every spawned worker imports the package) and about a millisecond a picture of executor traffic, so a handful of files gains nothing; a real run does — measured over the same archives, 1.85 s of thread pipeline becomes 1.38 s warm, and the gap widens with everything that loads the parent's GIL (a bigger library's probes, a reader thread, near-dups).

A process may not send a decoded picture back (it is 4.7 MB pickled against ~10 KB for everything else), so prepare_source_slim returns the ANSWERS — the near-dup verify and the orientation record read the bundle's own small vectors — and Importer._ingest_image decodes the file again only for the rare exact-pixel film-frame check. Both paths are asserted to produce identical libraries, down to every metadata row.

Lazy: nothing is imported until the iterator is consumed. Abandoning it keeps what was already imported, like the run itself.

The zeros ARE the precision: 19750000 is the year 1975 and nothing narrower, and a range query over it stays an integer comparison.

A picture's perceptual hash — the one thing this library compares when it asks whether two pictures are the same one.

File.phash is the stored form of this (a hex string, and it stays a string: scripts read it and the golden pins it). Phash.of(image) is how a consumer gets one for pixels that are NOT in the library — a video frame it just decoded, a derived copy it just made — so that its idea of "the same picture" is the importer's idea rather than a second one. Pair it with Library.phash_threshold and the two agree by construction.

docs.title: open_library
docs.text:
open_library(data_dir: Union[str, Path, None] = None, *, mode: str = 'r+', user: str = '', source: str = 'cli', busy_timeout: float = 30.0) -> 'Library'

Open the library at data_dir (default ./_data).

Reads like gzip.open / shelve.open / sqlite3.connect, and works as a context manager::

with open_library("/path/to/library") as lib:
    ...

mode="r" makes every mutator raise ReadOnlyError before touching the database — the guarantee the old read-only API gave, kept as an option.

user is recorded against everything this session changes, so the History view can say who did it; without one, scripted changes are anonymous. source is the badge beside them — "cli" means a local process against the library, which is what a script is.

transaction()

import_file(path, *, move: bool = False, **options)

Import ONE local file, and say where it landed.

There is no destination-group argument: the result carries the item, so put it where you want it after::

got = lib.import_file("/inbox/a.jpg", move=True)

Import bytes a caller already has — a download, an archive reader.

docs.title: add_file_urls
docs.text:
add_file_urls(rows) -> int

Record many web-URL sources in one transaction — the crawl batch.

rows is (file, url, accessed_at) triples (File handles or ids; accessed_at a datetime, an ISO string, or None), with File.add_url's own rules per row: idempotent per (file, url, access time), an offset-aware time stored as the UTC moment it names. One revertible History entry for the batch; returns how many rows were new. The singular File.add_url stays the shape for a one-off — this is for the loop that would otherwise pay an ops round-trip per file.

docs.title: assign_tags
docs.text:
assign_tags(pairs) -> int

Assign many (item, tag name) pairs in one transaction.

Items are Item handles or ids; names follow the tag-field rules (a leading - is the negative sign) and go through the ordinary assignment door — an alias assigns its target, a refused name (a minted score tag) is skipped rather than failing the batch. Pairs the item already carries are left alone. One revertible History entry; returns how many assignments were new. Item.tags.add stays the shape for a one-off.

docs.title: importing
docs.text:
importing(**options)

An import run for sources discovered one at a time:

with lib.importing() as run:
    for data, url, when, name in downloads():
        got = run.add(ImportBytes(data=data, name=name))
        if got.file:
            got.file.add_url(url, accessed_at=when)

ImportRun.add takes paths too, and ImportRun.add_many is the fast shape when the sources can be listed up front: it decodes and hashes ahead on worker threads and yields the same per-source results.

docs.title: reindex_metadata
docs.text:
reindex_metadata() -> int

Re-read what EVERY FILE of every item says about itself, then rebuild each item's index from its active one. Returns how many FILES were read (it used to return items).

THE ONE SURVIVING REPAIR: a library whose files were stored before every path that creates a file indexed its metadata has an index for the ACTIVE files alone. The four backfill CLI commands are gone by policy and none comes back, so this is reachable from a script and nowhere else.

It does NOT clear pins or mutes — those are answers somebody gave about which of several files to believe, and no amount of re-reading bytes can produce them again.

docs.title: query
docs.text:
ItemSet — a lazy, composable set of items.

Django's QuerySet is the idiom every Python user already knows for exactly this object, and the alternative — the bare generator the old API returned — cannot be counted, sliced, re-run, or bulk-mutated.

Iteration streams in WINDOWS, and prefetch is what makes a 50k-item walk affordable: before a window is yielded, each named relation is bulk-loaded for the whole window through the loaders the app already uses, so item.tags inside the loop is a dict lookup rather than a query.

tag_boxes() -> dict

Every box on every matching item: {item id: {tag name: [Box]}}.

The boxes come back as STORED — geometry in the item's REFERENCE frame, and a range-only box carrying a time and no rectangle. Map a rectangle through item.active_file.crop to get the frame the stored pixels actually show.

A name whose assignment is NEGATIVE on that item is present too: the boxes are keyed by tag name, and whether the tag applies is a different question — item.tags answers it.

docs.title: settings
docs.text:
The settings that shape the LIBRARY, not one person's view of it.

The tag prefixes decide what the app invents when it mints a tag for a subject, a place or an event, and the face threshold decides what lands in the shared catalog — so both are global, and a script that creates subjects has to be able to read them. Language, date format and the double-click actions are per-user preferences and are deliberately absent.

Small, immutable, and none of them a database row. PartialDate is the one that carries real weight: this library's dates know how much of themselves is known, and a datetime cannot say "1975, month unknown".

One per-item tag group, flattened — what ItemSet.tag_groups() hands back for a whole result at once.

A frozen record rather than an ItemTagGroup handle, because the point of the bulk read is that nothing here costs another query: tags is already the positive names in placement order, subjects already the display names. item.tag_groups is the live, editable view of the same thing.

docs.title: Phash
docs.text:
Phash(value: int)

A picture's perceptual hash — the one thing this library compares when it asks whether two pictures are the same one.

File.phash is the stored form of this (a hex string, and it stays a string: scripts read it and the golden pins it). Phash.of(image) is how a consumer gets one for pixels that are NOT in the library — a video frame it just decoded, a derived copy it just made — so that its idea of "the same picture" is the importer's idea rather than a second one. Pair it with Library.phash_threshold and the two agree by construction.

docs.title: PartialDate
docs.text:
PartialDate(value: int)

A date that knows how much of itself is known.

Stored as the sortable integer this library uses — YYYYMMDD for a subject's or an event's date, YYYYMMDDHHMMSS for a capture time — with zeros for whatever is unknown. The zeros ARE the precision: 19750000 is the year 1975 and nothing narrower, and a range query over it stays an integer comparison.

docs.title: taken_to_stored
docs.text:
taken_to_stored(value) -> Optional[int]

What item.taken = … writes: None to fall back, -1 for NEVER, else the sortable integer. The ops layer widens a date-width value to the column's own YYYYMMDDHHMMSS (db.normalize_taken), so a PartialDate of either width stores the same date.

docs.title: stored_to_taken
docs.text:
stored_to_taken(value: int) -> PartialDate

A stored 14-digit capture date, as the PartialDate a reader expects.

A capture date that carries no time IS a date, so it comes back at date width — which is what makes item.taken == PartialDate.parse("2019-04") hold after the round trip, and what hands partialdate.bounds (which reads the 8-digit encoding) a value it can answer for. One with a real time keeps its full width; midnight and "no time" are the same value, the price the encoding's own docstring already names.
